topic: Damaging Effects of Circulatory Arrest During Hypothermia
stem: Regarding the damaging effects of circulatory arrest during hypothermia, which statement about the **relative tolerance of organs** is correct?

choices.text: Brain's safe time is shortest; the kidney is occasionally damaged when the brain is not
The kidney has the shortest safe arrest time, and the brain is damaged only after the kidney
The spinal cord is more susceptible to ischemic injury than the brain is
At any temperature, the liver has a shorter safe arrest time than the kidney
Organs other than the brain are not damaged even by long periods of arrest

explanation.text: The ==brain== has the **shortest safe circulatory arrest time** of any organ or region, although the **kidney** occasionally seems to be damaged when the brain is not.

head: Organ
Tolerance of circulatory arrest (source)
rows: Shortest safe arrest time of any organ or region
Less susceptible to ischemic injury than the brain
Safe time longer than the brain's, shorter than the liver's (at any temperature)
60 min of arrest at 20°C–22°C: no structural or functional abnormality
explanation.caption: Organs and circulatory arrest

explanation.text: "Longer safe time" does not mean "immune": other organs **can be severely damaged** by long periods of arrest.
It is generally agreed that the brain has the shortest safe circulatory arrest time of any organ or region of the body
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 34

choiceNotes.b: It is generally agreed that the **brain** has the shortest safe arrest time; the kidney is only **occasionally** damaged when the brain is not.
choiceNotes.c: The spinal cord is **less** susceptible to ischemic injury than the brain (no deficits after arrest intervals of up to 60 minutes).
choiceNotes.d: At any temperature, the safe arrest time for the kidney is **shorter** than for the liver (and longer than for the brain).
choiceNotes.e: Other organs **can be severely damaged** by long periods of circulatory arrest; their safe arrest times are simply longer than the brain's.

topic: Brain Function and Structure: Risk Factors for Damage
stem: A neonate sustains brain injury in the setting of hypothermic circulatory arrest. How is this damage **most likely** to manifest, and what explanation does the source propose?

choices.text: Diffuse global injury, because all neonatal neurons are uniformly vulnerable to ischemia
Specific intellectual deficits, because cortical receptor density peaks in the neonatal period
Paraplegia, because the neonatal spinal cord is the region most sensitive to ischemia
Focal motor deficits, because receptor density in the motor cortex is highest at birth
Seizures or choreoathetosis, possibly related to high basal ganglia receptor density

explanation.text: In neonates, infants and small children, brain damage with circulatory arrest is more likely to show as ==seizures or choreoathetoid movements==; in adults, as **specific intellectual or motor deficits**.

steps.text: Density of specific membrane receptors varies with **age**
Receptors **transiently high in the basal ganglia** in the neonatal period
steps.label: neonate

steps.text: **Selective neuronal vulnerability** of these neuron groups
**Choreoathetosis** after ischemic injury in the very young
steps.label: ischemia

explanation.title: Definition
explanation.text: **Selective neuronal vulnerability** = a heightened sensitivity of specific neuron groups to ischemic injury.

Concentration of these receptors is transiently high in the basal ganglia in the neonatal period, which may relate to the appearance of choreoathetosis as a result of ischemic injury in the very young.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 34

choiceNotes.a: Brain damage with hypothermic circulatory arrest is **rarely diffuse**; the source invokes **selective** neuronal vulnerability of specific neuron groups.
choiceNotes.b: Specific intellectual or motor deficits are the usual pattern in **adults**; the receptor concentration that is transiently high in neonates is in the **basal ganglia**.
choiceNotes.c: The spinal cord is **less** susceptible than the brain; no trunk or limb deficits occur after arrest intervals of up to 60 minutes in infants.
choiceNotes.d: Focal (specific motor) deficits are the **adult** pattern; the source does not describe a neonatal peak of receptors in the motor cortex.

source.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass
source.loc: p. 34, Brain Function and Structure: Risk Factors for Damage

stem: An aortic arch repair is planned with the brain cooled to **15°C–20°C**. Based on the animal experiments and clinical experience cited in the source, which statement about the **duration of circulatory arrest** is correct?

choices.text: Arrest of 45 minutes has been securely shown to be free of damage
Brain ATP stays at its initial level throughout a 30-minute arrest
Arrest of 30 minutes or less is tolerated without evident damage
Brain ATP fails to recover on reperfusion after a 30-minute arrest
Arrest of 60 minutes at 15°C–18°C is consistently free of damage

explanation.text: When the brain is cooled to ==15°C–20°C==, circulatory arrest of ==30 minutes or less== is tolerated **without evident structural or functional damage**.

explanation.caption: Temperature and duration (brain at 15°C–20°C)
head: Arrest duration
What the source reports
rows: Tolerated without evident damage; ATP falls to 35% of initial values but **returns rapidly to normal** on reperfusion
Associated with **irreversible** structural or functional damage, though tolerated by some subjects under some circumstances

explanation.text: In experimental studies, **histologic** anoxic brain damage was found in **all** animals after 45–60 minutes of hypothermic arrest, although some survived without evident functional abnormality.
A fall in ATP during a 30-minute arrest is expected; what matters is its **rapid recovery** during reperfusion.
when the brain is cooled to 15°C to 20°C, circulatory arrest of 30 minutes or less is tolerated without development of evident structural or functional damage.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 34

choiceNotes.a: Evidence that circulatory arrest of **45 minutes** at these temperatures is safe is **less secure**.
choiceNotes.b: ATP concentrations **decline to 35%** of initial values during such a period.
choiceNotes.d: ATP **returns rapidly to normal** during reperfusion after such a period; failure of ATP recovery (2 of 4 animals) was seen after **60 minutes** of arrest.
choiceNotes.e: Arrest of **60 minutes or more** at 15°C–18°C is associated with **irreversible** structural or functional damage, although some subjects may tolerate it.

source.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: According to the source's synthesis on the safe duration of circulatory arrest, which finding is the **most sensitive indicator** that an arrest period was not completely safe?

choices.text: An evident postoperative functional neurologic deficit
Failure to reach electrocerebral silence on EEG before the arrest
Histologic CNS changes, even without functional abnormality
Postoperative renal failure requiring dialysis
Abnormal postoperative liver function tests

explanation.text: ==Histologic changes in the central nervous system==, without functional abnormalities, are the **most sensitive indicators** of lack of complete safety of an arrest period.

head: Indicator of damage
Sensitivity
rows: Less sensitive: may be absent despite histologic damage

explanation.text: In experimental studies, histologic anoxic brain damage was found in **all** animals after 45–60 minutes of hypothermic arrest, although some survived **without evident functional abnormality**.

explanation.title: Definition of safe
explanation.text: Fig. 2.9 defines "safe" arrest as the **absence of structural or functional damage**, so survival without a deficit does not prove the arrest was harmless.
histologic changes in the central nervous system, without functional abnormalities, are the most sensitive indicators of lack of complete safety of the arrest period used
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 42

choiceNotes.a: Functional abnormality is **less** sensitive: animals with histologic damage after 45–60 minutes could survive without evident functional abnormality.
choiceNotes.b: Electrocerebral silence is a **cooling endpoint** indicating minimal cerebral metabolic demand, not an indicator of damage from the arrest.
choiceNotes.d: The kidney's safe arrest time is longer than the brain's, and postoperative renal failure is mainly attributed to low cardiac output and CPB effects.
choiceNotes.e: The liver tolerates arrest longer than the kidney or brain (60 minutes at 20°C–22°C causes no abnormality).

stem: A 70-year-old man has postoperative confusion, agitation and transient parkinsonism **without localizing signs** after ascending aorta and arch replacement with 65 minutes of hypothermic circulatory arrest. The symptoms resolve before discharge. Which statement about this complication is correct?

choices.text: Arrest duration and increasing age are incremental risk factors for it
It is uncommon, occurring in fewer than 2% of survivors
Its prevalence is similar with arrest shorter or longer than 60 minutes
It has no long-term significance once it has resolved
It is unrelated to arrest duration in pulmonary thromboendarterectomy

explanation.text: This is ==temporary neurologic dysfunction (TND)==; its incremental risk factors are **duration of hypothermic circulatory arrest** and **increasing patient age**.

children: Up to **20%** of survivors of thoracic aortic operations with arrest

explanation.text: "Temporary" does not mean "harmless": TND is a marker for long-term functional neurologic deficit.
Incremental risk factors associated with developing this complication are duration of hypothermic circulatory arrest and increasing patient age.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 35

choiceNotes.b: Temporary neurologic dysfunction can occur in **up to 20%** of survivors of thoracic aortic operations using hypothermic circulatory arrest.
choiceNotes.c: Its prevalence **increases substantially** when the arrest exceeds 60 minutes (Fig. 2.2).
choiceNotes.d: TND is a **marker for long-term functional neurologic deficit**; although not permanent, it can be an important complication.
choiceNotes.e: In pulmonary thromboendarterectomy, arrest times **over 50 minutes** were a powerful risk factor for postoperative delirium.

stem: Neurologic complications of aortic arch surgery are categorized as permanent (PND) or temporary (TND) neurologic dysfunction. Which definition matches the source?

choices.text: PND: confusion or delirium that resolves before discharge, with a normal brain CT
TND: a focal embolic stroke with a corresponding CT defect that improves before discharge
PND: a focal or global deficit with CT defects that persist at discharge
TND: a global deficit (coma) with corresponding CT defects persisting at discharge
PND: any deficit present on the first postoperative day, whatever the CT findings

explanation.text: ==PND== = a **focal** (embolic stroke) or **global** (coma) deficit with corresponding **CT defects persisting at discharge**; ==TND== = non-focal dysfunction that **resolves before discharge** with a usually normal CT.

head: PND
TND
explanation.caption: Neurologic complications of aortic arch surgery

explanation.title: P vs T
explanation.text: **P**ND = **P**ersists at discharge with **P**ictures (CT defects); **T**ND = **T**ransient, CT clean.
PND is defined as either a focal (embolic stroke) or global (coma) deficit with corresponding defects on CT scans that persist at discharge from the hospital.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 39

choiceNotes.a: Confusion or delirium that resolves before discharge with a usually normal CT describes **TND**.
choiceNotes.b: TND is a **non-focal** neurocognitive dysfunction, and CT scans are usually **normal**.
choiceNotes.d: A global deficit (coma) with persisting CT defects is **PND**.
choiceNotes.e: PND requires a focal or global deficit with **corresponding CT defects** that **persist at discharge**.

source.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: In a reported series of 218 young patients undergoing repair of VSD, tetralogy of Fallot, transposition or AV septal defect with hypothermic circulatory arrest (mean arrest about 42 minutes, mean temperature 19.7°C in both groups), how did the **cooling method** relate to major neurologic events?

choices.text: Events occurred only after surface cooling to 28°C followed by core cooling
Event rates were similar, because arrest time and temperature were matched
Core cooling alone was safer, because it shortened the time before arrest
The excess events after core cooling reflected longer arrest times in that group
Events occurred only after core cooling alone, not after surface cooling first

explanation.text: Major neurologic events occurred in ==6% with core cooling by CPB alone== and in **0%** with **surface cooling to 28°C followed by core cooling**.

items: In neonates and infants, **rapid** core cooling was associated with more neurologic deficits than **more prolonged** core cooling.
In this series, **no** major event occurred when arrest lasted **less than 45 minutes**; the probability rose as arrest time increased beyond this (Fig. 2.6).

explanation.text: Table 2.2 **excludes seizures** followed by uneventful convalescence from major neurologic events.
A reasonable presumption is that the more rapid core cooling resulted in uneven cooling of the brain.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 35

choiceNotes.a: The reverse: surface cooling to 28°C then core cooling had **0** major events; core cooling alone had **8 (6%)**.
choiceNotes.b: Despite similar arrest times and temperatures, the rates differed: 0% vs 6% (P = .03).
choiceNotes.c: Core cooling alone had **more** events; the presumption is that more rapid core cooling caused **uneven** brain cooling.
choiceNotes.d: Mean arrest times were essentially equal: 42.5 minutes (surface then core) vs 42.8 minutes (core only).

topic: Cerebral Blood Flow During Cooling and Rewarming
stem: Cerebral blood flow and metabolism are measured in children during cooling before hypothermic circulatory arrest. Which **pre-arrest** finding suggests particular vulnerability to cerebral injury?

choices.text: A parallel fall in cerebral blood flow and cerebral oxygen consumption
Preserved flow–metabolism coupling at low temperature under alpha-stat
Electrocerebral silence on EEG for 3 minutes before the arrest
Low arterial pressure during CPB, now firmly established as causal
Increased cerebral oxygen extraction before the circulatory arrest

explanation.text: Children with ==increased oxygen extraction before circulatory arrest== may be particularly vulnerable to cerebral injury: flow was probably **inadequate for metabolic requirements**.

steps.text: **Cooling**: cerebral blood flow and O~2~ consumption fall **in parallel**
Cerebral blood flow probably **inadequate** for metabolic requirements

explanation.text: In **3 of 4** patients later found to have neurologic injury, oxygen extraction before the arrest was **increased**.

explanation.title: Usual physiology
explanation.text: Cerebral blood flow generally decreases with temperature during cooling, and coupling with metabolism is maintained even at low temperatures under the **alpha-stat** strategy.
patients with increased oxygen extraction before circulatory arrest may be particularly vulnerable to cerebral injury
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 35

choiceNotes.a: A **parallel reduction** in cerebral oxygen consumption and blood flow is what normally occurs during cooling.
choiceNotes.b: Coupling maintained at low temperatures with alpha-stat management was the usual finding, not a marker of vulnerability.
choiceNotes.c: In one study, electrocerebral silence for 3 minutes before arrest accompanied the **longest** recorded safe arrests in adults; it is not a marker of vulnerability.
choiceNotes.d: The role of hypotension during CPB in neurologic dysfunction **now appears less certain**.

source.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass
source.loc: p. 35, Cerebral Blood Flow During Cooling and Rewarming

topic: Cerebral Blood Flow During Cooling and Rewarming
stem: Which statement about **cerebral blood flow during rewarming** after hypothermic circulatory arrest is correct?

choices.text: It is reduced, yet jugular saturation suggests adequate O~2~ delivery in infants
It rises above baseline, producing hyperemia as soon as rewarming starts
It is reduced in experimental animals but not in humans
It is reduced only after circulatory arrest, never with continuous CPB
It is reduced, and jugular venous saturation shows inadequate oxygen delivery

explanation.text: Cerebral blood flow is ==reduced during rewarming== after circulatory arrest; in infants, **jugular venous oxygen saturation** suggests oxygen delivery is still **adequate**.

items: **Experimental**: flow is reduced during rewarming after arrest (Fig. 2.3).
**Humans**: occurs during cardiac surgery **with or without** arrest, and may affect outcomes.
**Infants**: reduced immediately after arrest **and** after achieving normothermia.

explanation.title: Fig. 2.3
explanation.text: In gerbils, flow during rewarming was **lower** after 48 minutes of total cessation of cerebral blood flow at 18°C than after continued hypothermic perfusion.

In one study of adults undergoing elective CABG (with or without valve replacement), the **severity of postoperative cognitive decline** was related to a **greater arteriovenous oxygen content difference** (radial artery vs jugular venous blood) **during rewarming**, which was associated with **low jugular venous saturation** and **low cerebral blood flow**.
In infants, cerebral blood flow is reduced during rewarming immediately after hypothermic circulatory arrest and after achieving normothermia.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 35

choiceNotes.b: Experimental and clinical studies show cerebral blood flow is **reduced**, not increased, during rewarming after arrest.
choiceNotes.c: The phenomenon **occurs in humans** during cardiac surgery and may affect outcomes.
choiceNotes.d: It occurs in humans **with or without** circulatory arrest.
choiceNotes.e: In infants, based on jugular venous oxygen saturation, oxygen delivery **appears adequate** during this period of reduced flow.

stem: Brain tissue glucose is increased, as is usual, at the start of a planned period of hypothermic circulatory arrest. By which mechanism does the source suggest this may **damage tissue** during the arrest?

choices.text: It raises cerebral oxygen extraction before the arrest begins
It shifts the brain toward alkalosis during the arrest period
It promotes red cell sludging and the no-reflow phenomenon
It fuels excessive glycolysis, with lactic acid accumulation
It restores glutamate reuptake, overexciting its receptors

explanation.text: Increased tissue glucose at the start of arrest may lead to ==excessive glycolysis and acidosis== during the arrest, possibly causing **tissue damage from lactic acid accumulation**.

steps.text: **Increased tissue glucose** at the start of arrest (usual)

explanation.title: Practical consequence
explanation.text: This possibility makes it **imprudent** to use glucose solutions for priming the pump-oxygenator and for intravenous infusion when a period of circulatory arrest is contemplated.

The biochemical milieu is incompletely understood: arterial **pH and PCO~2~** during cooling may affect brain tissue directly or via cerebral blood flow, but any effect on neurologic outcome is **uncertain**.
increased tissue glucose, such as is usually present at the beginning of the arrest period, may lead to excessive glycolysis and acidosis during the arrest period
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 36

choiceNotes.a: Increased oxygen extraction before arrest suggests **inadequate cerebral blood flow** for metabolic needs; the source does not attribute it to glucose.
choiceNotes.b: The concern is the opposite: **acidosis** from lactic acid accumulation.
choiceNotes.c: No-reflow relates to vascular changes and red cells in the perfusate (eliminated by hemodilution); the glucose concern is **glycolysis and acidosis**.
choiceNotes.e: Glutamate injury occurs when energy-dependent reuptake is **compromised**, not restored; it is not the glucose mechanism.

source.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: Which sequence best describes how **glutamate** contributes to neuronal injury during cellular energy depletion, such as cerebral ischemia during circulatory arrest?

choices.text: Excess reuptake -> glutamate depletion -> loss of excitation -> intracellular calcium falls -> cell death
Failed reuptake -> glutamate excess -> receptor blockade -> intracellular calcium falls -> cell death
Excess glycolysis -> glutamate synthesis -> lactic acid rises -> intracellular calcium falls -> cell death
Failed reuptake -> glutamate excess -> receptor overexcitation -> intracellular calcium rises -> cell death
Failed reuptake -> glutamate excess -> receptor overexcitation -> calcium rises -> apoptosis only

explanation.text: When energy is depleted, the **energy-dependent synaptic reuptake** of glutamate fails; ==glutamate accumulates==, overexcites its receptors, **intracellular calcium rises**, and neurons are injured and die.

steps.text: Neuronal injury and death (**necrosis and apoptosis**)

explanation.text: **Glutamate** is the major transmitter mediating synaptic excitation in the mammalian central nervous system; this process was seen in experimental animals after **2 hours** of circulatory arrest.

Experimentally, **apoptosis** (programmed cell death) has been demonstrated in the neocortex after hypothermic circulatory arrest (piglets, 90 minutes at 19°C), with damaged neurons seen **8 to 72 hours after reperfusion**.
Resulting overaccumulation of glutamate leads to excessive excitation of the glutamate receptors, leading to an increase in intracellular calcium and eventual neuronal cell injury and death.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 36

choiceNotes.a: Synaptic reuptake is energy dependent and is **compromised**, so glutamate **accumulates**; it is not depleted.
choiceNotes.b: Excess glutamate causes **excessive excitation** of its receptors and a **rise** in intracellular calcium.
choiceNotes.c: Glycolysis and lactic acid relate to increased tissue glucose, a separate mechanism; calcium **rises** in excitotoxicity.
choiceNotes.e: Glutamate excitotoxicity after hypothermic arrest mediates neuronal **apoptosis as well as necrosis**.

source.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: Neuronal necrosis after prolonged circulatory arrest is **selective**. Which brain regions are characteristically **most vulnerable** to excitatory amino acid injury?

choices.text: Superficial neocortex, brainstem and spinal cord
Hippocampus, cerebellum and basal ganglia
Frontal white matter, thalamus and pons
Neocortex alone, sparing deeper structures
Spinal cord gray matter and brainstem nuclei

explanation.text: The ==hippocampus, cerebellum and basal ganglia==, rich in **glutamate receptors**, are characteristically most vulnerable, implying **excitation** as an underlying mechanism.
Neuronal necrosis is **selective** and corresponds closely to the **distribution of excitatory amino acid receptors**.

children: Most vulnerable area to prolonged (> 70 min) arrest at 15°C (experimental histopathology)
Receptors transiently high in neonates -> choreoathetosis

explanation.text: The hippocampus, cerebellum, and basal ganglia, which have high concentrations of glutamate receptors, are characteristically most vulnerable to this injury, implying excitation as an underlying mechanism.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 36

choiceNotes.a: The source names the regions with **high glutamate-receptor concentration**: hippocampus, cerebellum and basal ganglia; the spinal cord is less susceptible than the brain.
choiceNotes.c: These are not the regions the source names; necrosis follows the distribution of excitatory amino acid receptors (hippocampus, cerebellum, basal ganglia).
choiceNotes.d: Neocortex is where **apoptosis** was shown in piglets; the characteristic excitotoxic targets are the hippocampus, cerebellum and basal ganglia.
choiceNotes.e: The spinal cord is less susceptible than the brain; the vulnerable regions are those rich in glutamate receptors.

stem: In a standardized study of 109 adults cooled for hypothermic circulatory arrest, which combination **prolonged** the time needed to reach electrocerebral silence on EEG?

choices.text: High hemoglobin, low arterial PCO~2~ and a slow cooling rate
Low hemoglobin, high arterial PCO~2~ and a rapid cooling rate
High hemoglobin, high arterial PCO~2~ and a rapid cooling rate
Low hemoglobin, low arterial PCO~2~ and a slow cooling rate
Low hemoglobin, high arterial PCO~2~ and a slow cooling rate

explanation.text: Time to electrocerebral silence was prolonged by ==high hemoglobin==, ==low arterial PCO~2~== and ==slow cooling rates==.

**Electrocerebral silence** = no electrical activity of cerebral origin at maximal gain (2 µV/mm). In this study it was reached at a mean nasopharyngeal temperature of **17.8°C** (range 12.5°C–27.2°C) after a mean of **27.5 minutes** of cooling (range 12–50).

explanation.title: Why it matters
explanation.text: In one study, the longest recorded durations of safe arrest in adults were when a full formal EEG had shown electrocerebral silence **for 3 minutes before the arrest**.
The time to cool to electrocerebral silence (Fig. 2.5) was prolonged by high hemoglobin concentration, low arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide, and slow cooling rates.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 37

choiceNotes.b: Each factor is reversed: **high** hemoglobin, **low** PCO~2~ and **slow** cooling prolonged the time.
choiceNotes.c: **Low** (not high) arterial PCO~2~ and **slow** (not rapid) cooling prolonged the time.
choiceNotes.d: **High** (not low) hemoglobin concentration prolonged the time.
choiceNotes.e: **High** hemoglobin and **low** arterial PCO~2~ prolonged the time.

source.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: A surgeon plans to start hypothermic circulatory arrest for adult aortic surgery as soon as the nasopharyngeal temperature reaches **18°C**, without EEG. Which statement best reflects the EEG data in the source?

choices.text: Virtually all adults show electrocerebral silence by a temperature of 18°C
Cooling to a set temperature is more reproducible than cooling to EEG silence
More than 30% of adults still show EEG brain activity at 18°C
The optimal temperature for circulatory arrest was determined to be 17.8°C
Electrocerebral silence is always reached once core temperature is below 10°C

explanation.text: Duration of cooling needed to reach electrocerebral silence is **variable** in adult aortic surgery: ==more than 30%== of patients still show brain activity on EEG at **18°C**, and in **10%** silence is not obtained even below 10°C.

items: In one study of 109 adults: mean temperature at silence **17.8°C** (range 12.5°C–27.2°C); only **60%** had silence by 18°C or 30 minutes of cooling.
**12.5°C** was sufficient to produce silence in **all** patients in that study.
In **10%** of patients, silence is not obtained even below **10°C**.

explanation.title: Endpoint vs number
explanation.text: Electrocerebral silence ideally indicates **minimal cerebral metabolic demand**; cooling to this endpoint gives a more reproducible effect than a fixed temperature, but the optimal arrest temperature was not determined.
more than 30% of patients exhibit brain activity on EEG even at a temperature of 18°C; in 10% of patients, electrocerebral silence is not obtained even after core temperature below 10°C.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 37

choiceNotes.a: Duration of cooling to electrocerebral silence is **variable**: more than 30% still show EEG activity at 18°C (in one study only 60% had silence by 18°C or 30 minutes of cooling).
choiceNotes.b: The reverse: cooling to an endpoint such as electrocerebral silence gives a **more reproducible** effect than cooling to a specific temperature.
choiceNotes.d: 17.8°C was the **mean** temperature at silence; the **optimal** temperature for arrest **could not be determined**.
choiceNotes.e: In **10%** of patients, electrocerebral silence is **not obtained** even below 10°C.

source.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: Why is EEG monitoring used **less often** nowadays to guide cerebral protection during thoracic aortic surgery?

choices.text: Its interpretation is fully automated and therefore insensitive
It is unaffected by anesthetic drugs, hypothermia or CPB
It needs a sonographer and an adequate small acoustic window
It samples only the anterior brain to a depth of 3 to 4 cm
It sees only superficial cortex and may miss deep ischemia

explanation.text: The EEG monitors only the ==superficial cortical layers on the crests of gyri== abutting the skull, so **deep (including subcortical) ischemia may be missed**.

explanation.title: Bottom line
explanation.text: For these reasons, EEG monitoring is used **less often** in clinical practice nowadays.

The **bispectral index (BIS)**, a 0–100 number from automated EEG analysis mainly used for awareness and depth of anesthesia, is used by some centers during thoracic aortic surgery but has the **same limitations as the standard EEG**.
the EEG monitors only the superficial layers of the cerebral cortex on the crests of gyri directly abutting the skull; ischemia in deep brain regions, including the subcortex, may be undetected.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 38

choiceNotes.a: The EEG test has a **subjective** nature of interpretation; automated EEG analysis describes the **BIS**.
choiceNotes.b: Anesthetic medications, hypothermia, CPB, prior ischemia and electrocautery **all affect** its sensitivity.
choiceNotes.c: Dependence on a sonographer and a small window is a limitation of **transcranial Doppler**.
choiceNotes.d: Monitoring mainly the anterior brain to a depth of 3–4 cm is a limitation of **NIRS**.

source.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: During aortic arch repair with antegrade cerebral perfusion (ACP) in a patient with an **incomplete circle of Willis**, the team considers transcranial Doppler (TCD). Which statement is correct?

choices.text: It measures middle cerebral artery flow but has no proven outcome benefit
It measures regional oxygen saturation of the anterior brain
Its routine use has been proven to improve outcomes after aortic surgery
It is operator-independent and needs no particular acoustic window
It detects gaseous emboli but cannot detect solid particles

explanation.text: TCD measures ==middle cerebral artery flow==, can help optimize ACP (especially with an incomplete circle of Willis) and detects emboli, but **no evidence** shows routine use improves outcomes.

head: Strengths
Limitations
rows: Expected to **optimize ACP**, especially with incomplete circle of Willis
Depends on images through a **small window**
explanation.caption: Transcranial Doppler

explanation.text: there is no evidence that the routine use of transcranial Doppler can improve clinical outcomes after thoracic aortic surgery, and its use remains largely experimental.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 38

choiceNotes.b: Regional oxygen saturation of the anterior brain is measured by **NIRS**.
choiceNotes.c: There is **no evidence** that routine TCD improves clinical outcomes; its use remains largely experimental.
choiceNotes.d: It requires a **sonographer's expertise** and depends on images acquired through a **small window**.
choiceNotes.e: TCD is a sensitive tool for detecting arterial particles, **both gaseous and solid**.

stem: Regional cerebral oxygen saturation is monitored with near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) during aortic arch surgery. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: It reliably reflects cerebral oxygenation during retrograde cerebral perfusion
It monitors the whole brain, including posterior and deep regions
Desaturation has been defined as a fall of more than 20% from baseline
It assumes that about 70%–75% of cerebral blood volume is arterial
Randomized trials have shown it to be superior to standard monitoring

explanation.text: Cerebral desaturation has been defined as a ==fall in regional cerebral oxygen saturation of over 20% from baseline==, yet **no threshold or duration** of NIRS-detected hypoxia is known to be tolerable.

children: Absorption of saturated vs unsaturated Hb

explanation.text: The definition of cerebral desaturation in cardiac surgery has been a decrease in regional cerebral oxygen saturation by over 20% from baseline.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 38

choiceNotes.a: NIRS is **inaccurate** for cerebral oxygenation with retrograde cerebral perfusion (RCP) during circulatory arrest.
choiceNotes.b: It primarily monitors the **anterior** brain, to a maximal depth of **3–4 cm**.
choiceNotes.d: It assumes **25%–30% arterial** and **70%–75% venous** blood, ignoring variability.
choiceNotes.e: **No randomized trials** have shown superiority of NIRS over standard monitoring.

Intact autoregulation, since cerebral volume is independent of blood pressure
Impaired autoregulation, but with no relation to outcome after arch surgery
Cerebral hyperperfusion, since COx measures middle cerebral artery flow
Impaired autoregulation, linked to higher hospital mortality and morbidity

stem: Preoperative contrast CT before aortic arch surgery shows **widespread protuberant, irregular-surfaced atheroma with few mural thrombi** throughout the aortic arch and thoracoabdominal aorta. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: This is leukoaraiosis, reflecting chronic ischemic damage to myelin and axons
Shaggy aorta is defined by abundant mural thrombus over smooth atheroma
Shaggy aorta can be diagnosed preoperatively only by brain MRI
Shaggy aorta, a risk factor for adverse brain or spinal cord outcomes
Highly shaggy lesions raise renal risk but not neurologic risk

explanation.text: This is ==shaggy aorta==; highly shaggy lesions in the aortic arch or thoracoabdominal aorta are **risk factors for adverse brain or spinal cord** neurologic outcomes.

The low-flow CPB group had the worse motor coordination and planning
Arrest was linked to worse motor coordination and planning, but not to lower IQ
Arrest was linked to worse overall neurologic status but normal motor skills
Arrest was linked to fewer speech abnormalities than low-flow CPB

stem: A colleague argues that **neonates tolerate hypothermic circulatory arrest better** than older patients, so longer arrest periods are acceptable in the very young. Which response is best supported by the source?

Disagree: little support; infants under 3 months with arrest scored below norms at 4 years
Agree: at 8 years, arrest and low-flow CPB groups had equivalent motor and speech outcomes
Agree: the very young have only transient seizures, without long-term consequences
Agree: age has no influence on neurologic outcome after arrest at any age

explanation.text: The claim that the very young suffer less brain damage from circulatory arrest has ==little factual support==.

items: Infants **younger than 3 months** who underwent arrest had importantly **reduced** cognitive, language and motor performance at **4 years** (vs general population).

stem: Focal neurologic damage (stroke) occurs in adults after hypothermic circulatory arrest. According to Ergin and colleagues, which combination of factors is related to it?

choices.text: Younger age, clot or atheroma in the arch, and longer arrest
Older age, clot or atheroma in the arch, and shorter arrest
Older age, clot or atheroma in the arch, and longer arrest
Younger age, absence of arch atheroma, and longer arrest
Older age only; arch disease and arrest duration were unrelated

explanation.text: Adult stroke after circulatory arrest is related to ==older age== (particularly beyond 60 years), ==clot or atheroma in the aortic arch==, and ==longer arrest duration==.

explanation.title: Age matters in adults
explanation.text: In adults with circulatory arrest, **increasing age** is an important predictor of **both stroke and TND**.

It typically appears within the first few hours after surgery
It correlates closely with the depth of cooling between 16°C and 20°C

stem: What is the basis for the recommendation that **arterial (perfusate) temperature not be reduced below 15°C**?

choices.text: Electrocerebral silence cannot be achieved at lower temperatures
Flow–metabolism coupling is lost below 15°C under alpha-stat management
Cold continuous perfusion at 10°C–15°C caused intellectual deficits in monkeys
Prolonged very cold perfusion at relatively high flow may cause choreoathetosis
Below 15°C, brain ATP cannot recover during reperfusion

explanation.text: Choreoathetosis may result from ==perfusion of the brain with very cold blood for a prolonged period at relatively high flows==; this is the basis for keeping arterial temperature **at or above 15°C**.

Choreoathetosis has occurred after hypothermic CPB **without** circulatory arrest. Continuous hypothermic perfusion at **10°C–12°C** produced moderate or severe brain damage, including choreoathetosis, in **10 of 16** patients (63%).

children: Continued metabolism in white matter and cerebellum

explanation.text: There are suggestions that this complication can result from perfusion of the brain with very cold blood for a prolonged period at relatively high flows.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 39

choiceNotes.a: Silence was reached in all patients by **12.5°C** in one study; it is not the basis of this recommendation.
choiceNotes.b: Coupling with cerebral metabolism is **maintained even at low temperatures** with alpha-stat management.
choiceNotes.c: Cold (10°C–15°C) continuous perfusion of brains already at 15°C caused **no** intellectual or other deficit in trained rhesus monkeys.
choiceNotes.e: The source does not link ATP recovery to perfusate temperature; failed ATP recovery was seen after **60 minutes** of arrest.

stem: Uneven brain reperfusion from the **no-reflow phenomenon** may contribute to choreoathetosis after circulatory arrest. What rationale for **hemodilution during cooling** does this support?

choices.text: It raises tissue glucose available for glycolysis during the arrest
No red cells in the perfusate before arrest eliminates no-reflow
It increases cerebral oxygen extraction before the arrest
It allows arterial temperature to be safely reduced below 15°C
It restores energy-dependent synaptic reuptake of glutamate

explanation.text: ==Absence of red cells== in the perfusion used just before circulatory arrest **eliminates the no-reflow phenomenon**, the rationale for **hemodilution during cooling**.

steps.text: No red cells in the perfusion just before arrest

choiceNotes.c: Increased oxygen extraction before arrest marks **vulnerability** to cerebral injury, not a benefit.
choiceNotes.d: The recommendation that arterial temperature not fall below 15°C is not changed by hemodilution in the source.

stem: An infant has **transient clinical and EEG seizures** early after repair of D-transposition of the great arteries with hypothermic circulatory arrest, then convalesces uneventfully. Which statement is best supported by the source?

choices.text: Being transient, such seizures show no link with later development
Such seizures occur in about half of patients undergoing arrest
Such seizures must be due to the arrest, as infants rarely seize otherwise
Such seizures were linked to worse neurodevelopment and to lower IQ at 4 years
Such seizures predicted worse outcomes at 1 year but higher IQ at 4 years

explanation.text: Although transient, early postoperative seizures were associated with ==worse neurodevelopmental outcomes== and **lower IQ at 4 years**.
Seizures were traditionally **not** counted as major neurologic events because they are usually transient; this does not make them harmless.

explanation.title: Other causes
explanation.text: Infants also seize from **thermoregulation and fluid balance disturbances** and **metabolic disorders** (especially glucose and calcium).
Because seizures are usually transient and followed by uneventful convalescence, they have not been considered major neurologic events.

choiceNotes.b: Early postoperative seizures have occurred in **5% to 10%** of patients undergoing hypothermic circulatory arrest.
choiceNotes.c: Infants are **highly susceptible** to seizures from other causes (thermoregulation, fluid balance, glucose and calcium disorders).

stem: A team planning neonatal repair reviews the evidence on the **duration of hypothermic circulatory arrest** and brain injury. Which statement is supported by the source?

choices.text: A 40-minute limit applies to adults, whereas infants tolerate 60 minutes
Arrest of ≥ 40 minutes is linked to brain injury in infants, children and adults
In infants, any arrest, however short, increases seizures over no arrest
Early Mayo Clinic experience found 60 minutes safe at a nasopharyngeal 20°C
In infants, seizure risk does not vary with the duration of the arrest

explanation.text: There is increasing evidence that intervals of hypothermic circulatory arrest of ==40 minutes or more== are associated with **brain injury in infants, children, and adults**.

explanation.caption: EEG-recorded seizures, neonates and infants < 6 months (one prospective study)
head: Arrest duration
Seizures

explanation.title: Early experience
explanation.text: Early experience at the **Mayo Clinic** suggested that **45 minutes** was the maximum safe duration even when nasopharyngeal temperature was reduced to 20°C.
In summary, there is increasing evidence that intervals of hypothermic circulatory arrest of 40 minutes or more are associated with brain injury in infants, children, and adults.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 40

choiceNotes.a: The association with brain injury is reported in **infants, children, and adults**; the idea that the very young tolerate arrest better has **little factual support**.
choiceNotes.c: With arrest of **40 minutes or less**, seizure occurrence was **similar** to that in patients without circulatory arrest (P = .38).
choiceNotes.d: Early Mayo Clinic experience suggested **45 minutes** as the maximum safe duration even at a nasopharyngeal temperature of 20°C.
choiceNotes.e: In a prospective study of infants younger than 6 months, arrest of **more than 40 minutes** was associated with more EEG-recorded seizures (24% vs 6.8%, P = .04).

stem: An infant repaired with 40 minutes of hypothermic circulatory arrest at 18°C has **adequate hemodynamics** but develops severe oliguria about 12 hours postoperatively. Which mechanism does the source implicate?

choices.text: Ischemic renal injury caused by the 40-minute arrest itself
Renal tubular apoptosis mediated by caspase 3 and caspase 8
Damaging effects of CPB, e.g. free hemoglobin and circulating toxins
Low cardiac output, the only cause of renal failure after arrest
Glutamate excitotoxicity in the renal tubules

explanation.text: When oliguria occurs despite adequate hemodynamics, ==damaging effects of CPB== must be implicated, for example **free hemoglobin and circulating toxins**.

steps.text: Arrest ≤ 60 min at 18°C–20°C does **not** damage the kidney (experimental)

branches.label: primary
branches.text: **Low cardiac output** before and after arrest

steps.text: Oliguria from about **12 h** postoperatively; renal failure

items: Free hemoglobin has been found in the **renal tubules** of some patients at autopsy.
Surface-induced arrest: **4 deaths (3%)** from renal failure among 130 patients.
Adults (distal arch, descending and thoracoabdominal aorta, mean 14.5°C, mean 38 min): dialysis in **2.6%**; **none** of 18 with preoperative creatinine > 1.5 mg/dL needed dialysis.

explanation.text: Free hemoglobin has been found in the renal tubules of some of these patients at autopsy.

choiceNotes.a: Experimentally, **60 minutes** of arrest at 18°C–20°C causes no morphologic or functional renal damage, so the arrest alone does not explain it.
choiceNotes.b: Caspase-mediated apoptosis is described in the **brain neocortex** of piglets, not as a cause of renal failure.
choiceNotes.d: Low output is the **primary** cause, but severe oliguria can develop when hemodynamics **appear adequate**.
choiceNotes.e: Glutamate excitotoxicity is a **neuronal** mechanism in the source, not a renal one.

stem: A surgeon plans **60 minutes** of hypothermic circulatory arrest at a nasopharyngeal temperature of **18°C**. According to the source's synthesis of safe arrest duration, what outcome should be expected?

choices.text: Essentially complete safety in nearly all patients
Permanent functional deficits in most patients
Evident functional damage in at least 70% of patients
Mostly structural damage; functional damage in only 10%–20%
No structural damage, but functional damage in most patients

explanation.text: After ==60 minutes at 18°C==, most patients have some **structural** evidence of damage, but only about **10%–20%** have evident **functional** damage, often transient.

head: Arrest at 18°C (nasopharyngeal)
Expected (Fig. 2.9)
rows: Safe in **at least 70%**; damage likely **structural**, without permanent functional sequelae
Most: some **structural** damage; **10%–20%** evident **functional** damage, often transient
explanation.caption: Probability of safe circulatory arrest

explanation.title: Think in probabilities
explanation.text: Safe arrest is best expressed as a **probability** of no structural or functional damage at a given temperature, not as an absolute value; the curves at 37°C, 28°C and 18°C are estimates, not rigorously derived.

Individual vulnerability varies widely and cannot yet be predicted from genetic or phenotypic profiles; early Mayo Clinic experience suggested **45 minutes** as the maximum safe duration even at a nasopharyngeal temperature of 20°C.

Most patients will have some structural evidence of damage from 60 minutes of arrest, but only about 10% to 20% will have evident functional damage, and in many of them, the manifestations will be transient.

choiceNotes.b: Only about **10%–20%** will have evident functional damage, and in many it is **transient**.
choiceNotes.c: About 10%–20% will have evident functional damage; **70%** relates to essentially complete safety at **45 minutes**.
choiceNotes.e: The reverse: **most** have structural evidence of damage; only a **minority** have functional damage.

stem: When deciding whether to use hypothermic circulatory arrest for a given operation, why must the team weigh it against **alternative perfusion strategies**?

choices.text: Continuous CPB, at any temperature, carries no potential for organ damage
Genetic or phenotypic profiles now identify who will tolerate long arrest
Circulatory arrest removes the need for a long period of CPB
Poor surgical exposure makes an inaccurate repair less likely
Arrest damage likely adds to damage from the long CPB it requires

explanation.text: The damage uniquely caused by circulatory arrest is ==likely additive== to that caused by continuous CPB, because a **long period of CPB** is required when arrest is used.

explanation.text: Perfusion strategies other than circulatory arrest are available for **essentially all** clinical cardiac surgical problems.

choiceNotes.a: Continuous CPB at normothermia or with moderate or deep hypothermia has **its own potential** for damaging organ systems.
choiceNotes.b: State-of-the-art medicine is **not yet capable** of defining such profiles to identify individual vulnerability.
choiceNotes.c: A **long period of CPB is required** when circulatory arrest is used.
choiceNotes.d: Inaccuracies are **more** likely when surgical exposure is poor.
